newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cousteau wrote of happiness, doom in memoires.
newsitem.headline: Cousteau wrote of happiness, doom in memoires.

text.p: French oceanographer Jacques-Yves Cousteau reveals his secrets for happiness, lessons on life and warnings of environmental hazards in his memoirs due to go on sale next Tuesday, six days after he died of a heart attack.
Cousteau wrote the 400-page "The Man, the Octopus and the Orchidea" over the course of 20 years, completing it shortly before dying on Wednesday at age 87.
Francine Cousteau has said that her husband, the man who showed the world that the ocean depths concealed a wealth of colour and fantasy, intended it as his testament.

"Bring a child into the world, write a book, put together a machine, build a chair -- those who create have the feeling to play a role bigger than themselves," Cousteau wrote in a chapter entitled "Happiness".
"Those who make no effort to create, who are unwilling to take a part of themselves to create a new entity will try in vain by other means to become something, but they will be nothing," he wrote.

On self-fulfilment, Cousteau said: "It takes generosity to discover the whole through others. If you realise you are only a violin, you can open yourself up to the world by playing your role in the concert."
The most passionate passages warn of the planet's devastation through nuclear energy, destruction of the ozone layer, overpopulation, arms production and the reign of money.
"It is absurd and even dangerous for those who live in prosperity to believe that the global economy is a cycle and its riches can and will circulate for ever."
"Unrenewable resources are being exhausted. Waste is building up. Goods that are valuable are disappearing while worthless rubbish thrives," Cousteau wrote.
"We must also urgently find a solution to the demographic explosion which has a direct influence on impoverishing the most underprivileged communities."

Cousteau, an outspoken environmentalist in his lifetime, accuses world leaders of irresponsibility and an obsession with money to the detriment of a clean and healthy environment, painting an apocalyptic picture of the destruction of the planet.
"They pocket benefits without looking ahead and write checks our descendants will pay for in the centuries to come," he wrote.

"With their pesticides and their pollution, their chemical discharges containing toxins along with the certainty of mutual destruction...with Bhopal in India, Three Mile island in the United States and Chernobyl in the Soviet Union -- with all their sinister errors, our scientific experts have hidden the hard reality from us: they simply determine if we and our children will live or die," Cousteau wrote.
